blocks.text: The strength (amplitude) of action potentials stays constant along the axon: the last one is as strong as the first. The speed of conduction, however, varies: it is greater when the axon is wider or myelinated.

In myelinated axons action potentials are produced only at the nodes of Ranvier and jump from node to node, skipping the myelinated stretches. This saltatory conduction is up to 50 times faster than in the fastest non-myelinated axons. In humans non-myelinated neurons conduct at 1 to 3 metres per second and myelinated neurons at up to 120 metres per second.

blocks.alt: Top: a non-myelinated axon with + charges outside and - inside except in one red active region where the charges are reversed; an arrow shows the active region moving on as the region behind repolarizes. Bottom: a myelinated axon with blue myelin segments and red curved arrows jumping from one node of Ranvier to the next. A note gives speeds of 1 to 3 m/s without myelin and up to 120 m/s with it.
blocks.caption: Saltatory conduction in a myelinated axon (original diagram after Figure 15.6).
blocks.long_description: An action potential does not itself travel: each active region depolarizes the next, which fires its own action potential, while the region behind repolarizes. Its strength stays the same along the axon. In a myelinated axon action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier and jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), up to 50 times faster than in the fastest non-myelinated axons.

blocks.prompt: Nerve impulses in neuron a travel faster than in neuron b. Give two possible reasons.
blocks.explanation: Neuron a is myelinated (saltatory conduction), or its axon is wider than b's.

items: Amplitude constant; speed higher with myelin or a wider axon. Saltatory: node to node, up to 50x faster; 1 to 3 m/s versus up to 120 m/s.
